q-79577.knowledge_point: Determining the Degree of a Homogeneous Polynomial
q-79577.source_problem: Is the function $f(x,y,z)=2xyz-{y}^{3}+{y}^{2}z$ homogeneous? If so, what is its degree?
q-79577.worked_solution:
A function $f(x,y,z)$ is homogeneous of degree $n$ if it satisfies the property

$$
f(tx,ty,tz)={t}^{n}f(x,y,z).
$$

So first, we compute $f(tx,ty,tz),$ and then we simplify by writing it as ${t}^{n}f(x,y)$ for some $n$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty,tz) & =2(tx)(ty)(tz)-(ty)^{3}+(ty)^{2}(tz) \\  & =2{t}^{3}xyz-{t}^{3}{y}^{3}+{t}^{3}{y}^{2}z \\  & ={t}^{3}(2xyz-{y}^{3}+{y}^{2}z) \\  & ={t}^{3}f(x,y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
f(tx,ty,tz)={t}^{3}f(x,y,z)
$$

and so the degree of the homogeneous function $f(x,y,z)$ is $3.$

q-79609.knowledge_point: Using the Properties of Linear Differential Operators to Identify Them
q-79609.source_problem:
Which of the following are linear differential operators?

- ${D}_{1}(y)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+y$
- ${D}_{2}(y)=x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-xy$
- ${D}_{3}(y)=y\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$
q-79609.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2})
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

Let's check each case in turn.

- The first operator is indeed linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{1}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2} \\  & =a[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{1}]+b[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{D}_{1}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{1}({y}_{2})\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- The second operator is also linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})-x(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =ax\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+bx\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-ax{y}_{1}-bx{y}_{2} \\  & =a[x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x{y}_{1}]+b[x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{D}_{2}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{2}({y}_{2})\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- The third operator is **not** linear.
To see why, we first evaluate the left-hand side of the linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{3}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})(a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}) \\  & ={a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+ab({y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}})\end{aligned}
$$

This is not the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
a{D}_{3}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{3}({y}_{2})=a{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.\,\times 
$$

q-79784.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE Using a Substitution
q-79784.source_problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=8x{y}^{1/2}-\frac{4}{x}y\,,\,y>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{1/2}.$*
q-79784.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1/2}\,⟹\,y={z}^{2}\,.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}=\frac{1}{2{y}^{1/2}}\frac{dy}{dx}\,⟹\,\frac{dy}{dx}=2z\frac{dz}{dx}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2z\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =8xz-\frac{4}{x}{z}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =4x-\frac{2}{x}z\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =4x-\frac{2}{x}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z & =4x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=4x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (4x) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =4{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z) & =4{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z)\,\text{d}x & =\int 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{2}z & ={x}^{4}+C \\ z & =\frac{{x}^{4}+C}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2} & =\frac{{x}^{4}+C}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & =\frac{({x}^{4}+C)^{2}}{{x}^{4}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-79799.knowledge_point: Identifying Solutions to Linear ODEs Using the Superposition Principle
q-79799.source_problem:
Given that ${y}_{1}(t)={e}^{-t}$ and ${y}_{2}(t)={e}^{4t}$ are solutions to the equation ${y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}-4y=0,$ which of the following must also be a solution to the equation?

- $y(t)={e}^{-t-1}$
- $y(t)=7{e}^{-t}-3{e}^{-4t}$
- $y(t)=\frac{{e}^{4t}}{4}$
q-79799.worked_solution:
According to the superposition principle, if the functions ${y}_{1}(t)$ and ${y}_{2}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous, linear differential equation, and ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ are constants, then $y(t)={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(t)$ is also a solution to the equation.

We're given that ${y}_{1}(t)={e}^{-t}$ and ${y}_{2}(t)={e}^{4t}.$ Therefore, the following function is also a solution:

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}
$$

Let's consider each option:

- The function $y(t)={e}^{-t-1}=\frac{{e}^{-t}}{e}$ is a solution of the given equation. Here, ${c}_{1}=\frac{1}{e},{c}_{2}=0.$

- The function $y(t)=7{e}^{-t}-3{e}^{-4t}$ is **not** a solution of the given equation because ${e}^{-4t}$ is not a solution.

- The function $y(t)=\frac{{e}^{4t}}{4}$ is a solution of the given equation. Here, ${c}_{1}=0,{c}_{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$

q-79847.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order Initial Value Problem Using a Substitution
q-79847.source_problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
(x+1)\frac{dy}{dx}=2{y}^{1/2}(x+1)^{3}+2y,\,y(0)=\frac{1}{4},\,x>-1.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z=(x+1)^{2}
$$

using the substitution $z={y}^{1/2}.$*
q-79847.worked_solution:
The substitution $z={y}^{1/2}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z=(x+1)^{2},
$$

with the initial condition

$$
z(0)=\sqrt{y(0)}=\frac{1}{2}\,.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=-\frac{1}{x+1},\,Q(x)=(x+1)^{2}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\int 1/(x+1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)^{-1}} \\  & =(x+1)^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>-1.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=(x+1)^{-1}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z) & =\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot (x+1)^{2} \\ \frac{1}{x+1}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\,z & =x+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x+1}\,z) & =x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x+1}\,z)\,\text{d}x & =\int (x+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{x+1}\,z & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+C \\ z & =(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+C)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we determine the value of $C$ that satisfies the initial condition $z(0)=\frac{1}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z(0) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ (0+1)(\frac{1}{2}{0}^{2}+0+C) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have 

$$
z=(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2})\,.
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z={y}^{1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2} & =(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2}) \\ y & =(x+1)^{2}{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-79945.knowledge_point: Finding a Series Solution to a Second-Order Initial Value Problem About a Non-Zero Point
q-79945.source_problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=\pi $, in ascending powers of $(x-\pi )$ up to and including the term in $(x-\pi )^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}={y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,y(\pi )=1,\,{y}^{′}(\pi )=-1.
$$
q-79945.worked_solution:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=\pi $:

$$
y(x)=y(\pi )+(x-\pi ){y}^{′}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(\pi )+⋯
$$

We're given $y(\pi )$ and ${y}^{′}(\pi ),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{″}(\pi )$ and ${y}^{(3)}(\pi ).$

We substitute $y(\pi )=1$ into the given equation to find ${y}^{″}(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(\pi ) & ={y}^{2}(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot (0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)=2y{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(\pi )$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(\pi ) & =2y(\pi ){y}^{′}(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+{y}^{2}(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =2(1)(-1)(0)+(1)^{2}(-1) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(\pi )+(x-\pi ){y}^{′}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(\pi )+⋯ \\  & =1+(x-\pi )\cdot (-1)+\frac{(x-\pi )^{2}}{2}\cdot (0)+\frac{(x-\pi )^{3}}{6}\cdot (-1)+… \\  & =1-(x-\pi )-\frac{1}{6}(x-\pi )^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

q-79950.knowledge_point: Finding a Series Solution to a First-Order Initial Value Problem
q-79950.source_problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=yx+{e}^{x},\,y(0)=0.
$$
q-79950.worked_solution:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{′}(0),$  ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=0,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =y(0)(0)+{e}^{0}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{″}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{″}(x)={y}^{′}x+y+{e}^{x}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{″}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & ={y}^{′}(0)(0)+y(0)+{e}^{0} \\  & =0+0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate ${y}^{″}(x)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)={y}^{″}x+{y}^{′}+{y}^{′}+{e}^{x}={y}^{″}x+2{y}^{′}+{e}^{x}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & ={y}^{″}(0)(0)+2{y}^{′}(0)+{e}^{0} \\  & =0+2(1)+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯ \\  & =0+x\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}\cdot 3+⋯ \\  & =x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

q-79951.knowledge_point: Finding a Series Solution to a First-Order Initial Value Problem
q-79951.source_problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=2x-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,y(0)=-1.
$$
q-79951.worked_solution:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{′}(0),$  ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=-1,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =2(0)-y(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{″}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{″}(x)=2-{y}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{″}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & =2-{y}^{′}(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+y(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =2-(1)(1)+(-1)(0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate ${y}^{″}(x)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)=-{y}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-{y}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & =-{y}^{″}(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+2{y}^{′}(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0+y(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =-(1)(1)+2(1)(0)+(-1)(1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

q-80467.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
q-80467.source_problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -8 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}∗ & 1 \\ ∗ & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$   find the first column of the matrix $P.$
q-80467.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$  

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=3.$ Computing $A-3I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -8 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 \\ 4 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 0 \\ 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$

q-80493.source_problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
q-80493.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

q-80496.source_problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}].$
q-80496.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

q-80766.knowledge_point: Finding Missing Constants in First-Order Partial Derivative Expressions
q-80766.source_problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
{f}_{x}(x,y)=y(1+x){e}^{x}+ax{y}^{3}+3{x}^{2},\,{f}_{y}(x,y)=bx{e}^{x}-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.
$$
q-80766.worked_solution:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y(1+x){e}^{x}+ax{y}^{3}+3{x}^{2}) \\  & =(1+x){e}^{x}+3ax{y}^{2}+0 \\  & =(1+x){e}^{x}+3ax{y}^{2} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(bx{e}^{x}-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}) \\  & =b(1+x){e}^{x}-6x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}(1+x){e}^{x}+3ax{y}^{2}=b(1+x){e}^{x}-6x{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $(1+x){e}^{x}$ and $x{y}^{2},$ respectively, we see that $b=1$ and $a=-2.$

q-80825.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues of a General 3x3 Matrix
q-80825.source_problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}].$
q-80825.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}+6\lambda +5)-(-1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}+7\lambda +6 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $6:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 3,\pm 6
$$

- Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}-7(1)-6 & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is not a root of the equation.

- Let's pick $x=-1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{3}-7(-1)-6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-1$ is a root of the equation.

So, we can factor $(\lambda +1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6$ using synthetic division:

| $-1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-7$ | $-6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $6$ |
|  | $1$ | $-1$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +1)({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.$

q-81202.knowledge_point: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degree of the Numerator is Greater
q-81202.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{2}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3+4{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}-x} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{4{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+4-2x)}{(1-\frac{1}{x})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}$ and $\frac{1}{x}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+4-2x)}{(1-\frac{1}{x})} \\  & ≈\frac{0+4-2x}{1-0} \\  & =4-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

q-81273.knowledge_point: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation
q-81273.source_problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}\,\,v \\ u+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$
q-81273.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}\,\,v$ and $y(u,v)=u+{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2uv & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={u}^{2} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2uv & {u}^{2} \\ 1 & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2uv\cdot 2v-{u}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =4u{v}^{2}-{u}^{2} \\  & =u(4{v}^{2}-u).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ u(4{v}^{2}-u) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equation $u(4{v}^{2}-u)=0$ defines a pair of intersecting curves in the $uv$-plane: the line $u=0$ and the parabola $u=4{v}^{2}.$

candidates.value: The critical points lie on the line $u=0$ and on the parabola $u=4{v}^{2}.$

q-81386.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Given Vectors Belong to the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
q-81386.source_problem:
Consider the linear transformation
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+4y \\ y+z \\ x-4z\end{aligned}]$ and the vectors

q-81386.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the vectors that belong to the kernel of $T$ are ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}.$

q-8306.knowledge_point: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by First Rearranging and Then Separating
q-8306.source_problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
q-8306.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2yx+y{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(2x+{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x+{x}^{2} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =2\int x\,\text{d}x+\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =\pm {e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=1$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =1 \\ K{e}^{{1}^{2}+{1}^{3}/3} & =1 \\ K{e}^{4/3} & =1 \\ K & ={e}^{-4/3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y={e}^{-4/3}\cdot {e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3}={e}^{({x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-4)/3}\,.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{-1/2} \\ f(9) & ={9}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{3} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{′}(9) & =-\frac{1}{2}(9)^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-1/2} & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}(x-9)+⋯ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x-9}{54}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=8$ into the above to approximate ${8}^{-1/2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{-1/2} & ≈\frac{1}{3}-\frac{8-9}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{54} \\  & =\frac{19}{54}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-83429.knowledge_point: Finding the Maclaurin Expansion of a Product of Functions Using Standard Maclaurin Expansions
q-83429.source_problem: Find the first three non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of ${x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$
q-83429.worked_solution:
The standard Maclaurin expansion for $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{5!}-⋯ \\  & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{120}-⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To get an expansion for ${x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ we multiply this series by ${x}^{2}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ={x}^{2}(x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{120}-⋯) \\  & ={x}^{3}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{7}}{120}-⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-83477.knowledge_point: Finding Global Maxima and Minima of a Function Whose Domain Is Piecewise Smooth
q-83477.source_problem: Find the global maximum of the function $f(x,y)=xy-x-y$ on the closed triangular region $D$ with vertices $(0,0),\,(2,0),\,(0,2).$
q-83477.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}y-1,\,x-1\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}y-1=0 \\ x-1=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ y=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(1,1).$ Since the point $(1,1)$ is not in the interior of $D$,  we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the line $y=2-x,$ in the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(2,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (0,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & =(t)(0)-(t)-(0) \\  & =-t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points on the open interval $t\in (0,1).$

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨0,t⟩,\,t\in (0,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(0,t) \\  & =(0)(t)-(0)-(t) \\  & =-t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points on the open interval $t\in (0,2).$

- The line connecting $(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨2,0⟩+t(⟨0,2⟩-⟨2,0⟩) \\  & =⟨2,0⟩+t⟨-2,2⟩ \\  & =⟨2-2t,2t⟩,\,t\in (0,1).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(2-2t,2t) \\  & =(2-2t)(2t)-(2-2t)-(2t) \\  & =-4{t}^{2}+4t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,1),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (-4{t}^{2}+4t-2)^{′} & =0 \\ -8t+4 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives one solution. Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain the candidate point $(1,1).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total we obtain four candidates:

$$
(0,0),\,(2,0),\,(0,2),\,(1,1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(2,0)$ | $(0,2)$ | $(1,1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $0$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | $-1$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-2$ at the points $(2,0),\,(0,2),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $0$ at the point $(0,0).$

q-83479.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}y,\,x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0,\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0).$ Since the point $(0,0)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(-2,4)$ and $(2,4)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,4⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,4) \\  & =(t)(4)-4 \\  & =4t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points in the open interval $t\in (-2,2).$

- The parabola connecting $(-2,4)$ and $(2,4)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨t,{t}^{2}⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,{t}^{2}) \\  & =(t)({t}^{2})-4 \\  & ={t}^{3}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

 
To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (-2,2),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{3}-4)^{′} & =0 \\ 3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives one solution $t=0$ inside the interval $t\in (-2,2).$
Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain one candidate point, $(0,0).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total we obtain three candidates:

$$
(0,0),\,(2,4),\,(-2,4)
$$

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(2,4)$ | $(-2,4)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-4$ | $4$ | $-12$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-12$ at the point $(-2,4)$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $4$ at the points $(2,4).$

q-83480.knowledge_point: Calculating an Eigenvector Corresponding to a Given Eigenvalue
q-83480.source_problem:
Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 3 \\ -9 & 7 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3.$
q-83480.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 3 \\ -9 & 7 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0 \\ -9{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{9}{5}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{5} & -\frac{2}{5} & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{5} & -\frac{2}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{5}(2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2{x}_{3}+3{x}_{3}) \\  & ={x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

q-83505.knowledge_point: Finding the Points at Which a Particle is Stationary Given the Acceleration Vector
q-83505.source_problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨8(1-2t)^{3},12(1+4t)^{2}⟩,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨-1,-26⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
q-83505.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨8(1-2t)^{3},12(1+4t)^{2}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 8(1-2t)^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int 12(1+4t)^{2}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-(1-2t)^{4}+{C}_{1},\,(1+4t)^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨-1,-26⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨-(1-2(0))^{4}+{C}_{1},\,(1+4(0))^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,-26⟩ & =⟨-1+{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-27.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨-(1-2t)^{4},\,(1+4t)^{3}-27⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨-(1-2t)^{4},\,(1+4t)^{3}-27⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need

$$
\begin{aligned}-(1-2t)^{4} & =0\,⇒\,t=\frac{1}{2}, \\ (1+4t)^{3}-27 & =0\,⇒\,t=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=\frac{1}{2},$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

q-8360.knowledge_point: Writing First-Order Linear ODEs in Standard Form
q-8360.source_problem:
Write the following first-order linear ODE in standard form.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=0\,.
$$
q-8360.worked_solution:
A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\operatorname{cot}⁡x & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{{2(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}y & ={{-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=2\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ and $Q(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$

q-8369.source_problem: Which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
q-8369.worked_solution:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property:

$$
f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\,
$$

The only option in which this is the case is

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

We can check this using one of two methods.

**Method 1**

Let $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}.$

We see that both the numerator and denominator are homogeneous polynomials of degree $2.$ Therefore, $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $2-2=0.$

Hence, the original differential equation is homogeneous.

**Method 2**

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write:

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}
$$

We can check that this is homogeneous showing that $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)^{2}-(tx)^{2}}{(ty)^{2}+(tx)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}-{t}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}+{t}^{2}{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})}{{t}^{2}({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ the original differential equation is homogeneous.

q-83710.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Corresponding Eigenvectors
q-83710.source_problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3$ are eigenvalues, and 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
q-83710.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & -1 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]

The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $A=PD{P}^{-1}.$
q-83854.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we get

$$

q-84046.knowledge_point: Finding the Y-Intercepts of a Hyperbola
q-84046.worked_solution:
To find the $y$-intercepts of the hyperbola, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the hyperbola and solve for $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =9 \\ 9(0)^{2}-{y}^{2} & =9 \\ -{y}^{2} & =9 \\ {y}^{2} & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot take the square root of a negative number. Therefore, the equation has no real solutions.
So, there are no $y$-intercepts.

q-84048.knowledge_point: Finding the Y-Intercepts of a Hyperbola
q-84048.worked_solution:
To find the $y$-intercepts of the hyperbola, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the hyperbola and solve for $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2}-\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ (0-3)^{2}-\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ 9-\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(y+2)^{2}}{2} & =8 \\ (y+2)^{2} & =16 \\ y+2 & =\pm 4 \\ y & =-6,2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $y$-intercepts are $(0,-6)$ and $(0,2).$

$$

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

In conclusion, we get $a=2,$ $b=13,$ and $c=3.$

q-85640.knowledge_point: Computing a Tangent or Cotangent Using the Pythagorean Identity
q-85640.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/97c98411b3455c78c9e061cf54fa76eabfccc369e9e364a5366eb58bd5d2935d.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $cos⁡\theta =\frac{2}{7},$ what is the value of $cot⁡\theta ?$
q-85640.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/8c7889d63cf5894236bc5f5e24feb64ecf5a47acb2c07c807a4e65458a991232.png)

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $sin⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $cos⁡\theta =\frac{2}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{2}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{4}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{45}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $sin⁡\theta $ is negative in the fourth quadrant. So, $sin⁡\theta =-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7}.$

Finally, knowing that $cot⁡\theta =\frac{cos⁡\theta }{sin⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
cot⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{2}{7})}{(-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7})}=-\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}=-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{15}.
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{5}{7}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, $sin⁡\theta =\frac{5}{7}.$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{5}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{5}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{25}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{24}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{24}}{7} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}.$

Finally, knowing that $sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(-\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7})}=-\frac{7}{2\sqrt{6}}=-\frac{7\sqrt{6}}{12}.

q-85966.knowledge_point: Calculating the Rate of Change of a Side Given the Rate of Change of the Volume
q-85966.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14096050/assets/8e03226558b1dbb2e93d23947b0b05f3d8413dc35207bbe9b536e68108f40955.png)

The length of a rectangular prism is decreasing by $3\,\text{cm}\text{/min},$ while the $5\,\text{cm}$ height does not change. If the volume of the rectangular prism is increasing at a rate of $15\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min},$  how fast is its width changing when its dimensions are $6\,\text{cm}$ in length and $2\,\text{cm}$ in width?
q-85966.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6\,\text{cm}, \\ y & =2\,\text{cm}, \\ z & =5\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-3\,\text{cm}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =15\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=6\,\text{cm},$ $y=2\,\text{cm}$ and $z=5\,\text{cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Since $z$ is not changing and $z=5,$ we get

$$
V=5xy.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5xy) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =5x(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+5y(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =5(6)(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+5(2)(-3) \\ 15 & =30(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})-30 \\ 45 & =30(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the width of the solid is increasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}/\text{min}$ at the moment when $x=6\,\text{cm},$ $y=2\,\text{cm}$ and $z=5\,\text{cm}.$

q-86413.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Negative Leading Coefficient
q-86413.source_problem: The equation $-4{w}^{2}-4w+11=0$ can be written in the form $4(w+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
q-86413.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-4{w}^{2}-4w+11) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 4{w}^{2}+4w-11 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{w}^{2}+4w-11 & =0 \\ 4({w}^{2}+w) & =11 \\ 4[{w}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}w+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}] & =11 \\ 4[{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{1}{4} & =11 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-1 & =11 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =11+1 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q=12.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =12 \\ {(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{12}{4} \\ {(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ \sqrt{{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{3} \\ |w+\frac{1}{2}| & =\sqrt{3} \\ w+\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \sqrt{3} \\ w & =-\frac{1}{2}\pm \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-86414.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Negative Leading Coefficient
q-86414.source_problem: The equation $-3{x}^{2}+36x-94=0$ can be written in the form $3(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q-p.$
q-86414.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-3{x}^{2}+36x-94) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-36x+94 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-36x+94 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-36x & =-94 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-12x] & =-94 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2}] & =-94 \\ 3[{(x-6)}^{2}-36] & =-94\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(x-6)}^{2}-3\cdot 36 & =-94 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2}-108 & =-94 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2} & =-94+108 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2} & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-6$, $q=14.$ Finally,

$$
q-p=14-(-6)=14+6=20.
$$

q-86415.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Negative Leading Coefficient
q-86415.source_problem: The equation $-4{w}^{2}+40w-75=0$ can be written in the form $4(w+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
q-86415.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-4{w}^{2}+40w-75) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 4{w}^{2}-40w+75 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{w}^{2}-40w+75 & =0 \\ 4{w}^{2}-40w & =-75 \\ 4({w}^{2}-10w) & =-75 \\ 4[{w}^{2}-2\cdot 5w+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2}] & =-75 \\ 4[{(w-5)}^{2}-25] & =-75\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w-5)}^{2}-4\cdot 25 & =-75 \\ 4{(w-5)}^{2}-100 & =-75 \\ 4{(w-5)}^{2} & =-75+100 \\ 4{(w-5)}^{2} & =25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q=25.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w-5)}^{2} & =25 \\ {(w-5)}^{2} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(w-5)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} \\ |w-5| & =\frac{5}{2} \\ w-5 & =\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ w & =5\pm \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =5+\frac{5}{2}=\frac{15}{2} \\ w & =5-\frac{5}{2}=\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $w=\frac{5}{2}$ and $w=\frac{15}{2}.$

q-86709.knowledge_point: Finding Global Maxima and Minima Given the Critical Points Inside the Function's Domain
q-86709.source_problem: Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=2xy+6x-3$ on the closed region $D$ enclosed by $y=-{x}^{2}$ and $y=-4.$ You are given that $f$ has a critical point at $(0,-3),$ and on the boundary of the region the points that could give rise to extreme values are $(-2,-4),$ $(-1,-1),$ $(1,-1),$ and $(2,-4).$
q-86709.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

**Step 1.** Find the critical points inside the region $D.$ 

To determine the critical points, let's first sketch the region:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14075482/assets/96096b5f8944785f1af1bbc4fd4942e081b4b3999887c0fa8d5d76008af454d5.png)

Since the point $(0,-3)$ is in the interior of $D,$ we include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.** Find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values.

In this case, we are *given* the points on the boundary of our region that could potentially be global extrema for $f.$ These are

$$
(-2,-4),\,(-1,-1),\,(1,-1),\,(2,-4).
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,-3) & =2(0)(-3)+6(0)-3 \\  & =-3 \\ f(-2,-4) & =2(-2)(-4)+6(-2)-3 \\  & =1 \\ f(-1,-1) & =2(-1)(-1)+6(-1)-3 \\  & =-7 \\ f(1,-1) & =2(1)(-1)+6(1)-3 \\  & =1 \\ f(2,-4) & =2(2)(-4)+6(2)-3 \\  & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-7$ at the points $(-1,-1)$ and $(2,-4),$

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $1$ at the points $(-2,-4)$ and $(1,-1).$

q-86712.knowledge_point: Finding Global Maxima and Minima of a Function Whose Domain Is Piecewise Smooth
q-86712.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093615/assets/20f279f5936987374965cbba01e7e089d88dae1c62767b1ab8eb9ebaea0e5ce9.png)

Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=6x-2xy$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2-{x}^{2}/2},$ shown above.
q-86712.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}6-2y,\,-2x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}6-2y=0 \\ -2x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,3).$ Since the point $(0,3)$ does not belong to the closed region of $D,$ we do not include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(-2,0)$ and $(2,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & =6(t)-2(t)(0) \\  & =6t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points in the open interval $t\in (-2,2).$

- The parabola connecting $(-2,0)$ and $(2,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨t,2-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,2-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =6(t)-2(t)(2-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}) \\  & ={t}^{3}+2t.\end{aligned}
$$

 
To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (-2,2),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{3}+2t)^{′} & =0 \\ 3{t}^{2}+2 & =0 \\ {t}^{2} & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation has no solution inside the interval $t\in (-2,2).$ So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points in the parabola connecting $(-2,0)$ and $(2,0).$

Finally, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total we obtain two candidates:

$$
(-2,0),\,(2,0)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(-2,0)$ | $(2,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-12$ | $12$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-12$ at the point $(-2,0)$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $12$ at the point $(2,0).$

q-86722.knowledge_point: Finding Global Maxima and Minima of a Function Whose Domain Is a Smooth Curve
q-86722.source_problem: Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=1-4xy$ on the closed elliptical region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}\le 9}.$
q-86722.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$  

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To do that, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}-4y,\,-4x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-4y=0 \\ -4x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0)\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=9.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =1-4(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =1-18\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =1-9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (1-9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{′} & =0 \\ -18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives four solutions, namely

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{3\pi }{4},\,\frac{5\pi }{4},\,\frac{7\pi }{4}\in (0,2\pi ).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{3\pi }{4},\,\frac{5\pi }{4},\,\frac{7\pi }{4}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain five candidate points:

$$
(3,0),\,(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}),\,(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}),\,(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}),\,(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(3,0)$ | $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ | $(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ | $(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ | $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-8$ | $10$ | $-8$ | $10$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-8$ at the points $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ and $(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $10$ at the points $(-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})$ and $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}).$

q-86758.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues of a General 3x3 Matrix
q-86758.source_problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$O=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].$
q-86758.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,O-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
O-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(O-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(O-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}0 & -1-\lambda  \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+1)+(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $2:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2
$$

Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}+2(1)^{2}-(1)-2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is a root of the equation. So, we can factor $(\lambda -1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2$ using synthetic division:

| $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-1$ | $-2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ |
|  | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -1)({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +2) & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda +1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

q-86975.knowledge_point: Approximating the Solution to an Initial Value Problem Using Euler's Method With One Step
q-86975.source_problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=5x+6y,\,y(0)=1
$$

Use Euler's method with one step to approximate $y(1).$
q-86975.worked_solution:
Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=1,$ we will use a step size of 

$$
Δx=1-0=1.
$$

First, we add the initial condition data:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  |  |

Next, we compute ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5x+6y \\  & =5\cdot (0)+6\cdot 1 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $6$ |  |

Next, we compute $Δy$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(6)\cdot 1 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $6$ | $6$ |

To get the values of $x$ and $y$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x$ and $Δy$ to $y,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =1+6 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these rows to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $6$ | $6$ |
| $1$ | $7$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(1)≈7.$

q-87289.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Two Events are Mutually Exclusive
q-87289.source_problem: Given $P(A)=\frac{1}{4},$ $P(B)=\frac{3}{10},$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{19}{40},$ determine whether $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.
q-87289.worked_solution:
To check if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, we must check that $P(A\cap B)=0.$

We can calculate $P(A\cap B)$ using the addition law:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ \frac{19}{40} & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{10}-P(A\cap B) \\ P(A\cap B) & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{10}-\frac{19}{40} \\  & =\frac{10+12-19}{40} \\  & =\frac{3}{40} \\  & \ne 0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A$ and $B$ are not mutually exclusive events.

q-87305.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Involving Mutually Exclusive Events
q-87305.source_problem: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events. Given that $P(B)=\frac{1}{15}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{3}{5},$ find $P(A).$
q-87305.worked_solution:
If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events, then $P(A\cap B)=0.$ 

Therefore, by the addition law, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B) \\ P(A) & =P(A\cup B)-P(B) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{15} \\  & =\frac{9-1}{15} \\  & =\frac{8}{15}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-87308.source_problem: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events. Given that $P(B)=\frac{18}{25}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{4}{5},$ find $P(A).$

$$

q-8854.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order ODE When the Right-Hand Side and the Complementary Solution are Dependent
q-8854.source_problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+16y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$
q-8854.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+16y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=P\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+4x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =8(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x)+16x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
8(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x)+16x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+16x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)\,=4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-8\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+8\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡4x) \\ -8\alpha =4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2}$, $\beta =0.$
Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}=P\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡4x-\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x.
$$

q-89417.knowledge_point: Calculating an Eigenvector Corresponding to a Given Eigenvalue
q-89417.source_problem:
Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3.$
q-89417.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}(2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4{x}_{3}-2{x}_{3}) \\  & ={x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.

q-89589.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Sums of Exponentials
q-89589.source_problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{4t}$ for $s>4.$
q-89589.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-2t}-{e}^{4t}} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}+L{-{e}^{4t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-2t}}-L{{e}^{4t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-2t}} & =\frac{1}{s+2},\,s>-2 \\ L{{e}^{4t}} & =\frac{1}{s-4},\,s>4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}-L{{e}^{4t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s-4} \\  & =\frac{(s-4)-(s+2)}{(s+2)(s-4)} \\  & =\frac{-6}{(s+2)(s-4)} \\  & =-\frac{6}{(s+2)(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{-2t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-2,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{4t}}$ is defined for $s\in (4,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(-2,\infty )\cap (4,\infty )=(4,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>4.$

q-89821.knowledge_point: Finding the Inverse Laplace Transform Using Partial Fractions
q-89821.source_problem: Find the inverse Laplace transform for $F(s)=\frac{10}{(s-2)(s+3)}.$
q-89821.worked_solution:
First, we write $F(s)$ as a sum of partial fractions, as follows: 

$$
\frac{10}{(s-2)(s+3)}=\frac{2}{s-2}-\frac{2}{s+3}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{1}{s-2},\,s>2 \\ L{{e}^{-3t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3},\,s>-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the addition property of the Laplace transform, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{s-2}-\frac{2}{s+3}} & =2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-2}}-2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+3}} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the inverse Laplace transform of $F(s)=\frac{10}{(s-2)(s+3)}$ is $f(t)=2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-3t}.$

q-90493.knowledge_point: Identifying Factors Giving an Exact ODE
q-90493.source_problem:
Consider the following differential equation:

$$
P(x,y)\text{d}x+5{y}^{4}{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}y=0
$$

Given that the differential equation is exact, which of the following functions could be $P(x,y)?$

- $10{y}^{5}{e}^{x}+4$
- $2{y}^{5}{e}^{2x}-y$
- $2{y}^{5}{e}^{2x}+{e}^{-x}$
q-90493.worked_solution:
A differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\text{d}y=0
$$

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we're given $Q(x,y)=5{y}^{4}{e}^{2x}.$ 

First, let's differentiate $Q(x,y)$ with respect to $x$:

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{y}^{4}{e}^{2x})=10{y}^{4}{e}^{2x}
$$

Now, let's apply $\frac{∂}{∂y}$ to each of the given options:

- First, we check $P(x,y)=10{y}^{5}{e}^{x}+4.$ This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(10{y}^{5}{e}^{x}+4)=50{y}^{4}{e}^{x}\ne \frac{∂Q}{∂x}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x,y)=10{y}^{5}{e}^{x}+4$ does *not* give an exact equation.

- Next, we check $P(x,y)=2{y}^{5}{e}^{2x}-y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{y}^{5}{e}^{2x}-y)=10{y}^{4}{e}^{2x}-1\ne \frac{∂Q}{∂x}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x,y)=2{y}^{5}{e}^{2x}-y$ does *not* give an exact equation.

- Finally, we check $P(x,y)=2{y}^{5}{e}^{2x}+{e}^{-x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{y}^{5}{e}^{2x}+{e}^{-x})=10{y}^{4}{e}^{2x}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x,y)=2{y}^{5}{e}^{2x}+{e}^{-x}$ gives an exact equation.

q-90706.knowledge_point: Constructing and Solving a Characteristic Equation
q-90706.source_problem: Consider the equation ${y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-6y=0$ where $y=y(x).$ If $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ is a solution, then $\lambda =$
q-90706.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}-6{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
(\lambda +2)(\lambda -3)=0,
$$

and so the solutions of the auxiliary equation  are $\lambda =-2$ or $\lambda =3.$

q-90725.knowledge_point: Identifying Non-Solutions of Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs
q-90725.source_problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}+8{y}^{′}+15y=0,$ which of the following **cannot** be $y(x)?$
q-90725.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+8\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+15{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +15) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +15 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
(\lambda +3)(\lambda +5)=0,
$$

and so the solutions of the auxiliary equation  are $\lambda =-3$ or $\lambda =-5.$

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{-3x}$ and ${e}^{-5x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only ${e}^{5x}$ is not a solution.
